sentence: Choose a respectful disagreement that explains your concern.
setupText: A colleague suggests opening the shop at six. You think there will be too few customers that early.
taskText: Choose a respectful disagreement that explains your concern.
text: A colleague suggests opening the shop at six. You think there will be too few customers that early. Choose a respectful disagreement that explains your concern.
options: I agree that six is a sensible time to open.
You don't understand our customers as well as I do.
I'm concerned that we won't have many customers at six.
We can discuss the opening time when everyone arrives.
answer: I'm concerned that we won't have many customers at six.
focusKey: coverage-register-b1-3041:Respectful disagreement focused on a proposal
explanation: This states a reservation about the proposal without attacking the person who suggested it.

rationales.I agree that six is a sensible time to o: This expresses agreement and leaves your concern unstated.
rationales.You don't understand our customers as we: This criticizes the colleague's knowledge instead of explaining the concern about demand.
rationales.I'm concerned that we won't have many cu: This states a reservation about the proposal without attacking the person who suggested it.
rationales.We can discuss the opening time when eve: This postpones discussion but does not communicate your disagreement or its reason.

sentence: Which request meets both requirements?
setupText: You need a supplier's price list no later than Wednesday. Your email should be courteous and keep the deadline clear.
taskText: Which request meets both requirements?
text: You need a supplier's price list no later than Wednesday. Your email should be courteous and keep the deadline clear. Which request meets both requirements?
options: Could you send the price list by Wednesday, please?
Could you send the price list whenever you have time?
You need to get that price list to me already.
Could you send the price list sometime after Wednesday?
answer: Could you send the price list by Wednesday, please?
explanation: The request form is courteous, and 'by Wednesday' preserves the latest acceptable date.

rationales.Could you send the price list by Wednesd: The request form is courteous, and 'by Wednesday' preserves the latest acceptable date.
rationales.Could you send the price list whenever y: This is polite but removes the Wednesday deadline.
rationales.You need to get that price list to me al: This sounds impatient and does not specify the actual deadline.
rationales.Could you send the price list sometime a: This politely requests delivery after the latest acceptable day.

sentence: Choose a professional complaint that states the known facts without guessing the cause.
setupText: A delivery was due on Monday. It is Wednesday and it has not arrived. You do not know why.
taskText: Choose a professional complaint that states the known facts without guessing the cause.
text: A delivery was due on Monday. It is Wednesday and it has not arrived. You do not know why. Choose a professional complaint that states the known facts without guessing the cause.
options: Your driver has clearly forgotten to deliver our order.
Our delivery was due on Monday and has not arrived.
You seem to have decided our order can wait.
The delivery may be late, but I'm not sure.
answer: Our delivery was due on Monday and has not arrived.
explanation: This records the missed date and current position without assigning an unsupported cause.

rationales.Your driver has clearly forgotten to del: This assumes the driver forgot, but the cause is unknown.
rationales.You seem to have decided our order can w: This attributes a decision to the supplier without evidence.
rationales.The delivery may be late, but I'm not su: This weakens a fact you know: the Monday delivery has not arrived by Wednesday.
rationales.Our delivery was due on Monday and has n: This records the missed date and current position without assigning an unsupported cause.

sentence: Choose an apology that accepts your error and identifies the correction.
setupText: You emailed the wrong file to a client. You now send the correct one.
taskText: Choose an apology that accepts your error and identifies the correction.
text: You emailed the wrong file to a client. You now send the correct one. Choose an apology that accepts your error and identifies the correction.
options: Sorry if you found the previous attachment rather confusing.
You opened the wrong file; please use this one instead.
The correct file will follow when I have located it.
Sorry I sent the wrong file. The correct one is attached.
answer: Sorry I sent the wrong file. The correct one is attached.
focusKey: coverage-register-b1-3044:Owning an error and supplying the remedy
explanation: This owns the mistake and directs the client to the replacement.

rationales.Sorry if you found the previous attachme: This apologizes conditionally for the client's experience without acknowledging that you sent the wrong file.
rationales.Sorry I sent the wrong file. The correct: This owns the mistake and directs the client to the replacement.
rationales.You opened the wrong file; please use th: This blames the client, although you sent the wrong file.
rationales.The correct file will follow when I have: This delays the correction instead of identifying the correct file you are sending now.

sentence: Choose the replacement that keeps the same meaning.
setupText: An official notice needs a more formal version of 'We have put off the workshop until May.'
taskText: Choose the replacement that keeps the same meaning.
text: An official notice needs a more formal version of 'We have put off the workshop until May.' Choose the replacement that keeps the same meaning.
options: We have cancelled the workshop planned for May.
We have arranged another workshop before May.
We have brought the workshop forward to May.
We have postponed the workshop until May.
answer: We have postponed the workshop until May.
explanation: 'Postponed' is a more formal alternative to 'put off' for moving an event to a later date.

rationales.We have cancelled the workshop planned f: 'Cancelled' means it will not take place as planned; the original moves it to May.
rationales.We have arranged another workshop before: This adds a different workshop and changes the time relationship.
rationales.We have postponed the workshop until May: 'Postponed' is a more formal alternative to 'put off' for moving an event to a later date.
rationales.We have brought the workshop forward to: 'Brought forward' moves an event earlier, the opposite direction from 'put off'.

sentence: Choose a courteous follow-up that repeats the question without accusing the venue of ignoring you.
setupText: You asked a venue about wheelchair access a week ago. You have not received a reply.
taskText: Choose a courteous follow-up that repeats the question without accusing the venue of ignoring you.
text: You asked a venue about wheelchair access a week ago. You have not received a reply. Choose a courteous follow-up that repeats the question without accusing the venue of ignoring you.
options: Why have you ignored my question about wheelchair access?
I take it your silence means wheelchair access is unavailable.
I'm following up to ask whether the venue has wheelchair access.
Thank you for confirming that your venue has wheelchair access.
answer: I'm following up to ask whether the venue has wheelchair access.
explanation: This refers to the earlier contact and repeats the needed question without assigning blame.

rationales.Why have you ignored my question about w: 'Ignored' assumes deliberate neglect, which you cannot infer just from the missing reply.
rationales.I take it your silence means wheelchair: This treats the lack of a reply as an answer and may lead to a false conclusion.
rationales.Thank you for confirming that your venue: This claims you received confirmation even though no reply arrived.
rationales.I'm following up to ask whether the venu: This refers to the earlier contact and repeats the needed question without assigning blame.

sentence: Choose a polite refusal that offers the available alternative.
setupText: A customer asks for delivery today. Today is fully booked, but tomorrow morning is available.
taskText: Choose a polite refusal that offers the available alternative.
text: A customer asks for delivery today. Today is fully booked, but tomorrow morning is available. Choose a polite refusal that offers the available alternative.
options: We can't deliver today, but we can come tomorrow morning.
We should be able to deliver today if you keep waiting.
You left it too late; tomorrow is your only chance.
We can't deliver today, so please contact a different company.
answer: We can't deliver today, but we can come tomorrow morning.
focusKey: coverage-register-b1-3047:Clear service refusal with an alternative
explanation: This clearly declines today's request while offering the specific available time.

rationales.We can't deliver today, but we can come: This clearly declines today's request while offering the specific available time.
rationales.We should be able to deliver today if yo: This creates an expectation of today's delivery despite the full schedule.
rationales.You left it too late; tomorrow is your o: This blames the customer and adds an unsupported claim that no later delivery is possible.
rationales.We can't deliver today, so please contac: This refuses the request but omits the alternative your own company can provide.

sentence: Choose a neutral subject line that describes the problem without alleging dishonesty.
setupText: Your invoice shows two charges for one room. You want the hotel to check whether there is an error.
taskText: Choose a neutral subject line that describes the problem without alleging dishonesty.
text: Your invoice shows two charges for one room. You want the hotel to check whether there is an error. Choose a neutral subject line that describes the problem without alleging dishonesty.
options: Your hotel's dishonest billing practices
Please explain why you overcharged me deliberately
Invoice query: two charges for one room
Thanks for correcting the room charges
answer: Invoice query: two charges for one room
explanation: This identifies the document and the discrepancy while leaving the cause open.

rationales.Your hotel's dishonest billing practices: This accuses the hotel of dishonesty before the charges have been checked.
rationales.Invoice query: two charges for one room: This identifies the document and the discrepancy while leaving the cause open.
rationales.Please explain why you overcharged me de: 'Deliberately' assumes an intention not established by the invoice.
rationales.Thanks for correcting the room charges: This presents the correction as completed when you are only requesting a check.

sentence: Which version keeps the promise to reply tomorrow?
setupText: You change 'I'll get back to you about your application tomorrow' into a more formal email sentence.
taskText: Which version keeps the promise to reply tomorrow?
text: You change 'I'll get back to you about your application tomorrow' into a more formal email sentence. Which version keeps the promise to reply tomorrow?
options: I will return your application to you tomorrow.
I will approve your application by tomorrow morning.
I will respond about your application tomorrow.
I will contact you about your application next week.
answer: I will respond about your application tomorrow.
focusKey: coverage-register-b1-3049:Formal paraphrase of get back to someone
explanation: 'Respond' expresses the intended meaning of 'get back to you' in more formal wording.

rationales.I will return your application to you to: This promises to send the application back, not to reply about it.
rationales.I will approve your application by tomor: This adds approval and a morning deadline, neither of which the original promises.
rationales.I will contact you about your applicatio: This keeps future contact but changes the promised day.
rationales.I will respond about your application to: 'Respond' expresses the intended meaning of 'get back to you' in more formal wording.

sentence: What is the chair politely asking people to do?
setupText: During a meeting, the chair says, 'It would help if we kept our comments brief; we have ten minutes left.'
taskText: What is the chair politely asking people to do?
text: During a meeting, the chair says, 'It would help if we kept our comments brief; we have ten minutes left.' What is the chair politely asking people to do?
options: Leave the meeting ten minutes before it finishes.
Make their remaining comments short.
Stop making comments for the rest of the meeting.
Write a short report after the meeting ends.
answer: Make their remaining comments short.
explanation: The indirect wording softens a request to limit speaking time; the ten-minute limit explains its purpose.

rationales.Leave the meeting ten minutes before it: The time explains the need for shorter comments, not an instruction to leave early.
rationales.Stop making comments for the rest of the: 'Keep our comments brief' allows comments but asks that they be short.
The indirect wording softens a request to limit speaking time; the ten-minute limit explains its purpose.
rationales.Write a short report after the meeting e: The chair refers to comments during the meeting, not a later written task.

sentence: Choose a tentative, cooperative suggestion.
setupText: Your team is discussing ways to reduce printing. You want to suggest sharing files online, leaving the decision open.
taskText: Choose a tentative, cooperative suggestion.
text: Your team is discussing ways to reduce printing. You want to suggest sharing files online, leaving the decision open. Choose a tentative, cooperative suggestion.
options: We have decided to share every file online from now on.
You must share your files online as I have explained.
Why haven't you started sharing the files online yet?
Perhaps we could share the files online instead.
answer: Perhaps we could share the files online instead.
explanation: 'Perhaps we could' offers a possible shared action without presenting it as an order or settled decision.

rationales.We have decided to share every file onli: This presents the idea as a decision already made.
rationales.Perhaps we could share the files online: 'Perhaps we could' offers a possible shared action without presenting it as an order or settled decision.
rationales.You must share your files online as I ha: This gives a requirement and invokes your authority instead of inviting discussion.
rationales.Why haven't you started sharing the file: This criticizes people for not implementing an idea they are still discussing.

sentence: Choose a polite question that checks that meaning.
setupText: A colleague says, 'Send it to the other office.' You are unsure whether they mean the North Street office.
taskText: Choose a polite question that checks that meaning.
text: A colleague says, 'Send it to the other office.' You are unsure whether they mean the North Street office. Choose a polite question that checks that meaning.
options: I'll send it to North Street, as you requested.
Do you mean the office on North Street?
Why can't you give clear instructions for once?
Could you send it to North Street for me?
answer: Do you mean the office on North Street?
explanation: This offers a possible interpretation and asks the speaker to confirm it.

rationales.Do you mean the office on North Street?: This offers a possible interpretation and asks the speaker to confirm it.
rationales.I'll send it to North Street, as you req: This acts on an uncertain interpretation as if it were confirmed.
rationales.Why can't you give clear instructions fo: This criticizes the colleague instead of checking the intended office.
rationales.Could you send it to North Street for me: This is polite, but it transfers the task to the colleague instead of clarifying the destination.

sentence: Which version preserves the warning about an unreliable printer?
setupText: You write a team memo about a printer: 'It's playing up again, so don't count on it.' The memo needs neutral, clear wording.
taskText: Which version preserves the warning about an unreliable printer?
text: You write a team memo about a printer: 'It's playing up again, so don't count on it.' The memo needs neutral, clear wording. Which version preserves the warning about an unreliable printer?
options: The printer has been repaired and is ready to use.
The printer has been removed from the office permanently.
The printer is faulty again, so it may not work reliably.
The printer is acting weird again, so don't bank on it.
answer: The printer is faulty again, so it may not work reliably.
explanation: This replaces the informal idioms with a clear statement of the fault and its practical consequence.

rationales.The printer has been repaired and is rea: This changes the warning into reassurance that the problem is resolved.
rationales.The printer has been removed from the of: This adds permanent removal, which the original does not state.
rationales.The printer is acting weird again, so do: This retains conversational idioms instead of making the wording neutral and clear.
rationales.The printer is faulty again, so it may n: This replaces the informal idioms with a clear statement of the fault and its practical consequence.

sentence: Choose a neutral report that preserves the customer's dissatisfaction without judging their manner.
setupText: A customer said the queue was too long. A staff member wrote, 'The customer whined about the wait.'
taskText: Choose a neutral report that preserves the customer's dissatisfaction without judging their manner.
text: A customer said the queue was too long. A staff member wrote, 'The customer whined about the wait.' Choose a neutral report that preserves the customer's dissatisfaction without judging their manner.
options: The customer enjoyed talking about the waiting time.
The customer complained about the length of the queue.
The customer complained in a childish way about the wait.
The customer asked where the queue started that morning.
answer: The customer complained about the length of the queue.
focusKey: coverage-register-b1-3054:Neutral reporting verb versus dismissive labeling
explanation: 'Complained' records dissatisfaction without the dismissive judgment carried by 'whined'.

rationales.The customer enjoyed talking about the w: This reverses the negative reaction by presenting the conversation as enjoyable.
rationales.The customer complained in a childish wa: 'In a childish way' retains the judgment about manner that the task asks you to remove.
rationales.The customer complained about the length: 'Complained' records dissatisfaction without the dismissive judgment carried by 'whined'.
rationales.The customer asked where the queue start: This changes a complaint about length into a question about location.

sentence: Choose an appreciative message suited to that relationship.
setupText: A close colleague covered your shift when you needed help. You send a warm personal text.
taskText: Choose an appreciative message suited to that relationship.
text: A close colleague covered your shift when you needed help. You send a warm personal text. Choose an appreciative message suited to that relationship.
options: Your assistance with the shift has been noted for the record.
Thanks for covering my shift. I really appreciate it.
Thanks, but you could have offered to cover sooner.
I'll need you to cover the same shift next week.
answer: Thanks for covering my shift. I really appreciate it.
focusKey: coverage-register-b1-3055:Warm gratitude in a close work relationship
explanation: This names the favor and expresses personal gratitude in a natural, warm tone.

rationales.Thanks for covering my shift. I really a: This names the favor and expresses personal gratitude in a natural, warm tone.
rationales.Your assistance with the shift has been: This sounds like an administrative record and does not convey the personal warmth requested.
rationales.Thanks, but you could have offered to co: The added criticism undermines the intended appreciative message.
rationales.I'll need you to cover the same shift ne: This makes a new demand rather than thanking the colleague for the favor.

sentence: Choose a helpful, polite response that directs the customer to the right team without promising a change.
setupText: You work at a sports center's reception. Only the bookings team can change a group reservation.
taskText: Choose a helpful, polite response that directs the customer to the right team without promising a change.
text: You work at a sports center's reception. Only the bookings team can change a group reservation. Choose a helpful, polite response that directs the customer to the right team without promising a change.
options: Please contact our bookings team about changing the reservation.
I'll change your reservation myself this afternoon.
That's not my job. Find someone from bookings.
The bookings team will definitely approve the change.
answer: Please contact our bookings team about changing the reservation.
focusKey: coverage-register-b1-3056:Helpful referral within a service role
explanation: This courteously identifies the team that handles changes without promising what it will decide.

rationales.I'll change your reservation myself this: This promises an action your reception role cannot carry out.
rationales.That's not my job. Find someone from boo: This identifies another team but sounds dismissive instead of helpful.
rationales.The bookings team will definitely approv: This guarantees an outcome that the situation does not establish.
rationales.Please contact our bookings team about c: This courteously identifies the team that handles changes without promising what it will decide.

sentence: Choose a polite refusal to discuss your salary.
setupText: At a work social event, someone asks how much you earn. You prefer to keep that private.
taskText: Choose a polite refusal to discuss your salary.
text: At a work social event, someone asks how much you earn. You prefer to keep that private. Choose a polite refusal to discuss your salary.
options: I don't remember, but I can check for you.
You must be earning less than I do here.
I'll tell everyone my salary when the others arrive.
I'd rather not discuss my salary, if you don't mind.
answer: I'd rather not discuss my salary, if you don't mind.
explanation: This states your preference and sets a boundary without criticizing the questioner.

rationales.I don't remember, but I can check for yo: This suggests you will provide the information later, rather than declining to discuss it.
rationales.I'd rather not discuss my salary, if you: This states your preference and sets a boundary without criticizing the questioner.
This speculates about the other person's pay and may sound competitive or insulting.
rationales.I'll tell everyone my salary when the ot: This offers to disclose the information, contrary to your wish for privacy.

sentence: Which version uses everyday language and keeps the same advice?
setupText: A shop wants simpler customer instructions. Its draft says, 'Retain your receipt in case you wish to return the item.'
taskText: Which version uses everyday language and keeps the same advice?
text: A shop wants simpler customer instructions. Its draft says, 'Retain your receipt in case you wish to return the item.' Which version uses everyday language and keeps the same advice?
options: Keep your receipt in case you want to return the item.
Return your receipt if you decide to keep the item.
Keep the receipt because the item must be returned.
Preserve the receipt should you elect to return the item.
answer: Keep your receipt in case you want to return the item.
explanation: 'Keep' and 'want' make the instruction plainer while preserving the possible reason for keeping the receipt.

rationales.Return your receipt if you decide to kee: This reverses both the receipt action and the reason for it.
rationales.Keep the receipt because the item must b: This turns a possible future return into a requirement.
rationales.Keep your receipt in case you want to re: 'Keep' and 'want' make the instruction plainer while preserving the possible reason for keeping the receipt.
rationales.Preserve the receipt should you elect to: This retains a formal style with 'preserve', 'should you', and 'elect', rather than simplifying it.

sentence: Choose a polite correction that clearly gives the right number.
setupText: A venue's email says your group has twelve people. Your booking confirmation says ten, which is correct.
taskText: Choose a polite correction that clearly gives the right number.
text: A venue's email says your group has twelve people. Your booking confirmation says ten, which is correct. Choose a polite correction that clearly gives the right number.
options: Just to clarify, our booking is for ten people, not twelve.
Thank you for confirming our booking for twelve people.
I suppose either ten or twelve people would be fine.
You really need to read your booking information properly.
answer: Just to clarify, our booking is for ten people, not twelve.
explanation: This introduces the correction courteously and states both the correct number and the error being corrected.

rationales.Thank you for confirming our booking for: This accepts the incorrect number instead of correcting it.
rationales.I suppose either ten or twelve people wo: This treats both numbers as acceptable, although the booking is for ten.
rationales.You really need to read your booking inf: This criticizes the reader without clearly supplying the correct number.
rationales.Just to clarify, our booking is for ten: This introduces the correction courteously and states both the correct number and the error being corrected.

sentence: Choose a polite interruption that asks for that clarification.
setupText: A meeting speaker is about to move to a new topic. You need to ask about the date they just mentioned.
taskText: Choose a polite interruption that asks for that clarification.
text: A meeting speaker is about to move to a new topic. You need to ask about the date they just mentioned. Choose a polite interruption that asks for that clarification.
options: Stop there. You haven't explained anything clearly today.
I'll explain the dates after you've finished your presentation.
Please carry on; I don't have any questions about that.
Sorry to interrupt, but which date did you mean?
answer: Sorry to interrupt, but which date did you mean?
explanation: This briefly acknowledges the interruption and asks the specific question before the topic changes.

rationales.Sorry to interrupt, but which date did y: This briefly acknowledges the interruption and asks the specific question before the topic changes.
rationales.Stop there. You haven't explained anythi: This attacks the speaker's overall explanation rather than politely asking about the date.
rationales.I'll explain the dates after you've fini: This announces your own later explanation instead of asking the question now.
rationales.Please carry on; I don't have any questi: This gives the speaker permission to continue and hides the clarification you need.
